channel.description: Recent content in Language on wid's blog

item.title: Rust Closures and Iterators
item.description: A closure is a struct whose fields are the values it captures, and whether its body reads, mutates, or consumes those values decides whether it is Fn, FnMut, or FnOnce. Iterator adapters only stack up structs that hold such closures; elements pass through the chain one at a time when a consuming method like collect calls next. The sixth post in a Rust study series.

item.title: Rust Memory Layout and Allocation
item.description: The same three-field struct takes 12 bytes when it keeps declaration order and 8 when the compiler picks the order. Option<&T> is 8 bytes like the pointer itself, with no tag, and a Vec keeps 24 bytes on the stack and its elements on the heap. Sizes were checked with size_of and the effect of removing allocations with criterion. The eighth post in a Rust study series.

item.title: Rust Smart Pointers
item.description: A linked list written as a plain enum fails with E0072, and an Rc sent to a thread fails with E0277. Box lifts the rule that sizes must be known at compile time, while Rc, RefCell, Arc, and Mutex each relax the one-owner, no-overlapping-borrows rule, paying with a heap allocation, count updates, run-time checks, or locking. The seventh post in a Rust study series.

item.title: Rust Traits, Generics, and dyn
item.description: Generics (including argument-position impl Trait) compile a copy of the function for each type it is called with and call it statically. dyn Trait compiles one function that reads the implementation’s address from a vtable. I treat the choice as depending on whether types must be mixed, and on whether the cost of extra copies or of indirect calls is the one that hurts. The fifth post in a Rust study series.

item.title: Rust Lifetimes
item.description: A lifetime annotation 'a does not make a value live longer. It is a contract stating which input a returned reference borrows from, and the borrow checker combines that contract with each reference’s last use to compute borrow regions. The fourth post in a Rust study series.

item.title: Rust References and Borrowing
item.description: A Rust reference borrows a value without taking ownership. The compiler allows many shared references &T or a single mutable reference &mut T at a time, rejecting code that changes a borrowed value, and it also rejects references that would outlive their owner, all at compile time. The third post in a Rust study series.

item.title: Rust Move, Copy, and Clone
item.description: In Rust, assignment and passing a function argument move ownership by default. Only Copy types are bitwise-copied and leave the original usable, and the cost of duplicating heap data shows up in the code as a clone() call. The second post in a Rust study series.

item.title: Rust Ownership and Freeing Memory
item.description: Rust has no garbage collector. Every value has a single owner, and the value is dropped where that owner’s scope ends. Because the drop point is fixed by scopes in the source code, files and locks are cleaned up by the same rule as memory. The first post in a Rust study series.

item.title: JPA Persistence Context and Dirty Checking
item.description: A managed entity from findById gets UPDATEd through dirty checking, with no save() call. The three entity states, how snapshot comparison works, what save() actually does, and the persistence context lifetime that all of it depends on.

item.title: @Transactional Only Works Through the Proxy
item.description: @Transactional doesn’t work just because it’s declared. Spring wraps the bean in a proxy and intercepts only the calls that go through it. Why the annotation is silently ignored on private methods and self-invocation, and how @DataJpaTest’s test transaction hides the defect.

item.title: Three Type Systems and Runtimes — JVM, CPython, and the Go Compiler
item.description: Java pairs static strong typing with JVM bytecode and adaptive JIT optimization. Python combines dynamic typing with an interpreter and declarative type hints. Go ships static structural typing and a single compiler. The type-system decision drives the runtime mechanism.

item.title: Three Concurrency Models — GIL, Virtual Thread, and Goroutine
item.description: CPython’s GIL serializes multithreaded execution and pushes work onto multiprocessing or asyncio. Java pinned threads 1:1 to the OS until virtual threads (Java 21) reopened the thread-per-request model. Go shipped with an M:N scheduler from day one. The model you start from decides whether your service goes thread-per-request, reactive, or multiprocess.

item.title: Three Garbage Collectors — How Java, Python, and Go Reclaim Memory
item.description: All three languages use a garbage collector, but the priorities differ. Java leans on generational + region GCs (G1, ZGC), Python combines reference counting with a cyclic detector, and Go runs a single concurrent tri-color mark-and-sweep. What each GC gave up is what shapes its operational profile.

item.title: Everything Is Pass by Value — Memory Transfer in Go, Java, and Python
item.description: Calling a function with an object is often described as pass by reference, but in memory all three languages copy values. Java copies a reference value, Python binds a new name to the same object (call by sharing), and Go copies a struct header — escape analysis decides where the values live.

item.title: Go Concurrency Model
item.description: Go’s concurrency model builds on CSP, providing Goroutines and Channels as core tools. An overview of how each works and when to choose what.

item.title: Spring WebFlux Fundamentals — Non-blocking I/O and the Reactive Stack
item.description: Spring MVC assigns one thread per request. When I/O waits pile up, threads sit idle. WebFlux replaces this with an event loop-based non-blocking model. A summary of the structural differences from MVC, the Reactor pattern, and when to choose which.

item.title: Nest.js Fundamentals — DI and Module System
item.description: Nest.js provides a DI container and Module system at the framework level in the Node.js ecosystem. A summary of its core design principles: IoC, DI, Module, and Provider.
